highlights.title: The Roman telescope has enough gas for 22 years, double NASA's expectations
highlights.summary: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is gliding toward its distant observation post on a pinpoint trajectory so precise that engineers estimate the spacecraft's fuel load will last twice as long as their initial expectations, the space agency confirmed Monday.
body: The $4.3 billion observatory’s designers originally planned to load enough propellant into Roman’s four fuel tanks for a minimum lifetime of five years, plus a potential five-year mission extension. That was a conservative estimate. NASA officials knew an on-target launch and perfect execution of the observatory’s first post-launch course correction maneuver would leave Roman with a hearty fuel reserve.

“As a result of exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team, brilliant execution by the operations team, and a precise launch from SpaceX, Roman has fuel for at least 22 years of potential science operations,” Jamie Dunn, center director at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, said in a press release.
The James Webb Space Telescope received a similar lifetime boost after a picture-perfect launch on a European Ariane 5 rocket in 2021.

highlights.title: AI ‘Actor’ Tilly Norwood Told Me That ‘All Lives Matter’
highlights.summary: The virtual character, which is promoting its upcoming movie Misaligned, tries to evade politics by repetitively commenting on the clothes you’re wearing.
body: For Hollywood stars, press junkets are an opportunity to promote new work while connecting with fans. They tell funny or embarrassing stories about one another, give us a glimpse into the film production process, and reveal mannerisms that make them more relatable.

So why would anyone want to talk to Tilly Norwood, an interactive, British-accented digital character and “actor” developed with generative artificial intelligence by Xicoia, an AI division of a studio called Particle 6 Group? It’s a fair enough question considering that it does not exist in our physical realm and will never appear in a movie that any halfway serious person would care about.

But Particle 6 recently claimed in an email that Norwood was “ready for absolutely anything!” What’s more, the company is allowing journalists access to the model without a handler to “keep the conversation on track.” So I decided to test whether Norwood could actually offer anything of substance.

body: While there are more details to uncover in other previews in the weeks heading up to the Nov. 19 launch, there are several major questions about GTA 6 that we still have no concrete answers for. Here are several of the biggest ones.

We've seen glimpses of Jason's house and Lucia's apartment in official footage of GTA 6, and we learned from previews that players won't be able to purchase additional houses. (According to Rockstar, it wouldn't make sense for a couple on the run to be constantly expanding their real estate portfolio, which makes sense.) Still, there is a lot that could happen in terms of customization of both these spaces, especially Jason's house, which appears to be in various stages of construction during the first two trailers.

We also know that you'll be able to alter Jason and Lucia's appearance through working out, sleeping, and diet choices. It's not clear if you'll be able to take this to extremes, or whether the changes will be relatively subtle, like with Arthur Morgan in Red Dead Redemption 2.

highlights.title: Masahiro Sakurai Forced to Abandon Game Designers Award After 16 Years as He Can't Find a Successor
highlights.summary: Masahiro Sakurai revealed that the Game Designers Award won’t return to the Japan Game Awards, as he has failed to find an adequate replacement to take up his mantle.
body: The Game of the Year Division of the Japan Game Awards took place yesterday, September 14, recognizing the best and brightest in Japanese game development. While numerous titles and creative minds were celebrated, one accolade is standing out from the rest — and that’s because it’s not coming back for future JGA shows.

Masahiro Sakurai, creator of Kirby and Super Smash Bros., founded the Game Designers Award in 2010. As told by the CESA’s official website, this award recognizes games based on their creativity and originality. Games that are considered for the award must incorporate “new ideas that are a clear departure from existing works” and “expand the form of game software by presenting new ways for the user to enjoy and play with the game.”

The Game Designers Award is ultimately granted to “the title that reached out to a wide range of people, including those who don't usually play games actively, and that made the memorable achievement of the year, will be selected as the award-winning title.”

highlights.title: The AI data center boom is colliding with cities scarred by big industry
highlights.summary: National outcry against data center construction has spread to Philadelphia, where officials suggested possible construction in a neighborhood already impacted by a now-defunct oil refinery.
body: Across the country, Americans are debating how their lives might change if new AI data centers are built in their backyards. Data center companies and their customers are promising new jobs and economic growth, but that pitch hasn’t won over a majority of Americans who oppose data center construction in their area, often over environmental and energy concerns.
For activist Shawmar Pitts, these concerns aren’t theoretical. He knows better than anyone what it’s like to live in the shadow of American industrialization.

A lifelong resident of the Grays Ferry neighborhood in Southwest Philadelphia, Pitts grew up next to what was then the East Coast’s largest oil refinery, which shut down after an explosion in 2019. Though many of his friends and family suffered from chronic health conditions, he didn’t realize what might have caused these illnesses until he encountered the environmental justice group Philly Thrive, which was tabling in his neighborhood in 2018 about a proposed oil refinery expansion.

highlights.title: How Competitive ‘Pokémon’ Inspired Author Ava Reid’s New Dystopian YA Series ‘Winterveil’
highlights.summary: It’s the start of another dark academia season and fantasy author Ava Reid (“A Study in Drowning,” “Innamorata”) is celebrating with the release of her new YA dystopian novel, “Winterveil.” The first book in a planned duology, “Winterveil” is set at Valeran Academy, which boasts the brightest – and…
body: “I, like so many of us, grew up playing ‘Pokémon’ as a kid,” Reid tells Variety. “Playing ‘FireRed,’ ‘LeafGreen.’ I have all my Pokemon plushies right behind me on my couch right now. But it was during the pandemic that I think so many of us got very involved in kind of esoteric hobbies, and my hobby that I got really into during COVID was competitive ‘Pokémon,’ specifically.”

And that’s what it sounds like, according to Reid, “’Pokémon’ where you play against you know other players and you have battles.” “And I’m talking specifically about the official competitive format of Pokemon, the one that’s run by the Pokémon Company itself,” Reid says. “There are different fan formats where you can play online, but the official competitive format is called VGC. So I got very, very into VGC, watching a bunch of kind of VGC content creators, playing on the in-game ladder myself.”

Reid’s time spent playing some hard core Pokemon inspired aspects of the competitive nature of the academy within “Winterveil,” a book that publisher HarperCollins has described as “The Secret History” meets “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.”

highlights.title: How Mariska Hargitay Pulled Off Her Fashion-Filled 2026 Emmys Hosting Gig
highlights.summary: “Let’s be honest, it’s a little terrifying,” says Harigtay of hosting. “But I’m in a season of my life where I’ve been presented with opportunities that terrified me a bit, so I thought, why not!”
body: Given the fact that Mariska Hargitay has been steering Law & Order: SVU for 27 years (!!) now, it’s safe to say she was the perfect choice to host the 2026 Emmys last night. She is, after all, a TV legend.

There was even more to celebrate: Hargitay was also the first woman to host the Emmys in 15 years. “When I first heard that, I was genuinely surprised,” Hargitay tells Vogue post-event. “Of course I understand the significance of it, and I’m incredibly proud to be that woman. But I also hope the next woman doesn’t have to wait another 15 years. There are so many brilliant, funny, fearless women who could stand on that stage.”

Her opening monologue certainly did not disappoint. “NBC is celebrating its 100th year, and I’ve been on Law & Order for all of them,” was one of many zingers. There were skits with Taylor Swift, and even a musical number with Andrew Rannells. “I love television,” Hargitay says. “I’ve spent so much of my life making it, and I very much understand how many people it takes to tell these stories and make them matter. So the idea of getting to stand in that room, and celebrate this community, felt incredibly special.”

"We don't need new laws or regulations," Huang said, adding that there should not be a "false choice" between the speed of innovation and the safety of AI products.
Nvidia is the biggest company in the world by valuation, with its profits having boomed as a result of rampant demand for the AI computing chips it makes.
Huang's stance on AI safety contrasts with those in the industry who have recently expressed fears that the technology could wipe out humanity.

body: The sensational Brook, after a summer without a Test hundred, crashed the ball to all parts in hitting 114 not out from 49 balls to power his side to 254-4.
His 10 fours and six sixes were ferocious - reminiscent of former England batter Pietersen, the newest addition to this side's backroom staff.
"I don't even think the genius of KP could come close to what Harry Brook has talent-wise," said Brook's former captain and team-mate Ben Stokes, who was watching on TV.
Brook was six years old when Pietersen - a shock appointment as a mentor through to next year's World Cup - secured England the Ashes on the final day at The Oval in 2005.

body: It's very Zack Snyder-y, as the ex-DC director is well-known for his slow-motion action shots that indulge in violence. Insomniac's last superhero game, Marvel's Spider-Man 2, also included this option. It allowed fans to capture beautiful web-swinging gameplay where time can briefly slow to highlight a graceful animation or a gorgeous shot. It's certainly a great way for creators to have full control over their gameplay for unique footage.
Marvel's Wolverine is officially out now after an extensive five-year wait. IGN gave the game a 6/10 in its review, noting that the game has strong bones, but lacks enough variety to sustain itself.

"Marvel's Wolverine's slick and satisfying combat wears thin well before its conclusion, so much so that even its strong character work can't quite save it from being anything more than okay," we said.

Insomniac Games has noted that it is listening to feedback from players in an effort to keep refining the experience and making it better after launch. Wolverine actor Liam McIntyre has managed to shrug off some of the harsh comments thrown at the game, stating that he's experienced backlash before and is proud of the game that the team made.

body: “It’s very tempting to attack your competitor and say these guys are unsafe,” he said. “But I think the more responsible way to respond to it is to say, let’s look at our own record. We may not have had this big, high-profile incident, but I’m sure we’re not perfect.”
Nvidia’s Jensen Huang countered not long after, “Run as fast as you can.”

Amodei is calling for three courses of action: embedding third-party evaluators inside AI companies, coordinating safety standards among Democratic countries and, eventually, larger global coordination. At Dreamforce, Amodei said Anthropic has committed to independent evaluators and is “going to have a dialogue with the rest of the industry” on the other two steps.

Amodei, xAI’s Elon Musk and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have all recently called for a slowdown in the pace of AI development. The comments from the CEOs follow warnings from Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic researcher, who resigned with a public declaration that AI could lead to the extinction of humanity within the decade. His comments have stirred a larger debate within Silicon Valley, gained the attention of regulators and alarmed the public.

highlights.title: Go with the flow: do you need to filter US tap water?
highlights.summary: Experts share best practices for considering water filters – whether you’re drinking municipally treated water or relying on a well. Americans have a lot of questions about their drinking water. How is it treated? What’s in it? Most importantly, is it safe?
body: “I’ve even been out to eat where people overhear me talking about my work and come over to ask me a question about their tap water,” said Kimberly Parker, an environmental engineer who studies chemical contaminants in drinking water at Washington University in St Louis.

Most Americans have access to municipal water, which “tends to be really well treated” and largely safe to drink, said Parker. Across the US, water is monitored for contamination via centralized infrastructure at federal and state levels.
In Parker’s experience, “many environmental engineers choose not to use filtered water” because of their informed confidence in the safety of tap water, she said.
Nevertheless, whether you’re drinking municipally treated water or relying on a well, there are water-safety challenges.

highlights.title: DOJ Takes Paramount’s Side Against States in Fight Over $1.9 Billion Bond
highlights.summary: The Department of Justice sided with Paramount on Tuesday, arguing that a coalition of 12 states should be forced to post a bond as the price of continuing to block the Warner Bros. merger.
body: The DOJ approved the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger in June and issued an unusual and lengthy statement explaining its support for the transaction. The 12-state coalition, led by California, reached the opposite conclusion in July, filing suit to prevent the merger from reducing competition in the theatrical and basic cable markets. A trial is scheduled to begin on March 2.

Paramount voluntarily agreed not to close the deal until after a trial is held back in July. At the time, Martinez-Olguin had issued a 28-day temporary restraining order, but had not imposed an injunction that would block the deal indefinitely.

Rather than fight an injunction motion — and potentially be forced to appeal an adverse ruling — Paramount chose instead to concede the issue and concentrate its trial defense. But the company had a change of heart in August, arguing that the states should be forced to post the bond or, in the alternative, allow the merger to proceed.
